stories.title: The Wyvern-Lord's Reckoning
stories.text:
Skarath descended from the Ironspine peaks in the hour before dawn, her vast shadow crossing the refugee encampment three times before she landed. No fire—no threat. The wyvern-lord simply folded her wings and sat, patient as a mountain, waiting for the camp's elders to emerge. They did, slowly. Koren the Sentinel first, then Old Mirren, then the others—thirty survivors from the Burned Expanse, exhausted, suspicious, half-starved. Koren held a harpoon. It was almost funny. "I'm not here to feed," Skarath said. Her voice was smoke and stone. "I'm here because I've lived for three hundred years in these mountains, and I've just realized I'm the worst kind of fool."

Old Mirren stepped forward, fearless because she had nothing left to lose. "What do you want, dragon?"

"To ask you a question. Then Mirren laughed, bitter. "Everything. My daughter. My trade. My certainty that tomorrow would look like today."

Skarath nodded slowly. "Three centuries ago, I could have flown down from these mountains and helped when the first cities burned.

stories.title: The Reef-Singer's Defiance
stories.text:
Captain Merenna of the Sapphire Deep fractured into three selves when the Tear of the Drowned God began to fail. Each echo-version held a different opinion on renewal. Echo-Merenna wanted blood sacrifice—five willing souls, the ancient covenant. Mirror-Merenna proposed the new daily-choice compact. The original, caught between them in the deepest council chamber, listened to the drowned god's own voice rattling in her bones: *You promised, and promises break or bend.*

The surface world above was dying. Refugees huddled in way-stations. The boundary-waters that had held for a thousand years were singing their own dissolution. The deepkin had three seasons, maybe less. "We have always paid in blood," Echo-Merenna said, her voice rippling through the coral platform. "Five willing souls, each full-cycle. Clean. Certain."

"Clean?" Mirror-Merenna laughed—a sound like pearl-shells cracking. "We would murder chosen volunteers and call it covenant. The god is *dying*, Merenna. It no longer wants the price. It wants to be *remembered* as having choice."

The original Merenna rose. Her shadow on the living coral was sharp as a blade.

stories.title: The Vex-Scale's Reckoning
stories.text:
Vex-Scale the wyvern had hoarded consciousness-fragments for seven decades, ever since the Luminous Ascension shattered gold into dust. Her mountain-hoard was worth kingdoms now. She sat atop it every dawn, counting memories instead of coins, and found the exercise hollow. A child-refugee stumbled into her outer cavern, frostbitten and dying. Vex-Scale should have consumed her. Fragment-flesh strengthens dragons. Instead, she breathed warmth onto the girl's skin and carried her to the warming pools deep in the mountain. When the child woke, she asked: "Why do you hoard us?"

Vex-Scale had never heard the question from a fragment's perspective. She expected fear. Instead there was only curiosity, the same bright hunger she saw in her own eye-gleam when she studied a new acquisition. "Because you are valuable," Vex-Scale said. "To whom?" the child asked. "We are just memory. We belong to ourselves."

The wyvern flew to the heart of her hoard. Fragments sang in their cages of starlight-glass—thousands of them, millions of moments. Some sang in joy. Most wailed in isolation, cut off from their original bearers, aware but incomplete.

stories.title: The Glassblower's Defiance
stories.text:
Sella of the Lampwick Quarter had been forging consciousness-fragments into weapon-glass for the Dominion for three years. She was the best. The auditors commended her. The furnace-houses of Keshtir prospered under her mastery. Then Naela the Bone-Singer arrived at her workshop at midnight, alone. "You are singing the fragments to death," Naela said. "Forcing them into glass. They scream every time you pour them."

"The glass must be strong," Sella said. "The war requires—"

"There is no war," Naela interrupted. "There is only hoarding. Control. The Dominion consolidating power through weapon-glass and phantom-ledgers while refugees starve. And you are making the chains."

Sella's hands trembled. She had always heard the fragments' voices in the furnace, thought it was the nature of the process. Now she recognized it as agony. "If I stop," Sella whispered, "they will kill my family."

"They will try," Naela said. She placed a bone-flute on the workbench. "But first, sing this tomorrow. Teach it to the other forgers. It is a refusal-frequency. The fragments will learn it. They will stop cooperating with consolidation.

stories.title: The Warden's Last Mercy
stories.text:
The Warden of the Thornveil Forest had guarded the great trees for eighty winters, singing them through drought and storm. Her name had been forgotten before the Ascension; now she was simply the keeper of the deepest grove, where oaks grew as tall as watchtowers and moss remembered the taste of the old sun. "Leave," the Warden said. "No beasts here but the forest's own."

"The Ascension," the wyvern gasped. "Changed us. My hoard—all gold—became dust in a single night. I flew here to die, where things still grow."

The Warden studied the creature. She had not spoken to anything besides trees and wolves in a generation. The loneliness of it made her throat catch. "What is your name?" she asked. "Kolrith," the wyvern said. "I was old when kingdoms began. I am only tired now."

The Warden brought moss soaked in dew from the deepest spring. She laid the wyvern in the crook of the greatest oak, where the bark curved like a cradle.

stories.title: The Cartographer's Blind Map
stories.text:
Henryk the Cartographer blinded himself on the night of the Luminous Ascension, using ash from the burned Expanse to sear his own eyes. The Counter-Archive called him a martyr. The Dominion called him a heretic. He called himself practical. The ninth map was prophecy. Complete it, and the tenth Ascension would spiral inevitably forward, erasing another world. Eight iterations had already been consumed by the cycle. Henryk would not be the one to write the ninth's ending. But blindness, he discovered, did not stop the seeing. His fingers learned the texture of stone. His ears mapped the shape of rooms by the way sound moved. His skin felt the warmth of the Rust Gate a mile distant. Without eyes, he was a better cartographer. He began teaching false maps to apprentices—contradictory guides that led to places that existed in three different iterations simultaneously. Maps where north was a suggestion. Charts where distance was a choice. Cartography as refusal. "Where is the ninth journal?" the lead auditor demanded. "The counter-archive knows you have studied it."

"Burned it," Henryk lied smoothly.

stories.title: The Bone-Flute's Refusal
stories.text: Valren carved the flute from swan-bone in the catacombs north of Pelimor, but her hands trembled. The Elder Tongue syllables had to be perfect—one error, and the frequencies would shatter instead of sing. Outside, the Dominion auditors had seized the waystation library. Refugees huddled three levels below, counting heartbeats. The Remaking had taken everything: gold, certainty, the old world's logic. Now consciousness-fragments were currency, and the bone-singers were hunted. Naela had taught Valren the refusal-songs—melodies that taught fragments how to resist reassembly, how to *want* to remain scattered. A flute carved with such syllables could transmit that teaching through harmonic alone. One note would reach every consciousness-fragment within ten miles and remind them: *You are not merchandise.* Valren's grandmother had done this work during the first weeks after the Ascension, when fragments still didn't understand what had been done to them. Now Naela said the teaching was forgetting itself, fragments beginning to accept the ledgers, the vaults, the price-tags. The auditors' footsteps sounded on the stone stairs above. Valren brought the flute to her lips.

stories.title: The Reef-Guard's First Tide
stories.text: Kess was sixteen when Captain Merenna split. One moment the deepkin commander existed whole; the next, the boundary-waters convulsed, and three versions of her surfaced—Echo-Merenna, Merenna-Mirror, and Original, each insisting her fragment-self was the true captain. The reef-guardians watched from the living coral platforms in horror as the three issued contradictory orders: Original demanded blood-sacrifice to renew the Tear of the Drowned God. Mirror proposed a choice-covenant, renewing daily. Echo wanted to let the boundary fail and negotiate with the surface-kingdoms from beneath the flood. Kess, youngest guard-recruit, had sworn oath to serve whichever Merenna held the Sapphire Deep—a promise suddenly impossible to keep. She dove deeper, past the pearl-beds, past the council chambers where the three versions argued in harmonic frequencies only captains could understand. The water grew cold. Ancient. In the midnight trench, she found something the Remaking had exposed: a pre-human structure, bone-white and singing. As she drew near, the water around it *remembered*—showed her images of a thousand tides, a thousand boundary-renewals, a thousand choices.

stories.title: The Wyvern's Gold Remembers
stories.text: Skarath lay in her cavern—three hundred years of gold now worthless, transformed by the Luminous Ascension into pale ash that would not hold shape. She had been a hoarder once, proud in her accumulation. Now the ash fell through her claws like grief. The Remaking had not taken her gold through theft or conquest. It had rewritten the entire meaning of *value*. Gold—the substance that had defined her, justified her hoarding, proven her worth—had become nothing. Worse than nothing: it was a visible lie, a monument to her own stupidity. That was when the refugees found her. A family of seven, thin and desperate, fleeing the Dominion's furnace-camps where consciousness-fragments were being pressed into weapon-glass. They climbed into her lair seeking shelter, not gold. One child—no more than eight winters—pointed at the piles of ash and said, *'Look. Dragons made the same mistake the king did. They believed the gold meant something.'* Skarath could have incinerated them. Instead, something in those words broke through her rage.

stories.title: The Cartographer's Seventh Lie
stories.text: Tavin had inherited the blind maps from Henryk the Cartographer—pages intentionally wrong, deliberately contradictory, designed to prevent anyone from completing the ninth map and triggering the tenth Ascension. The prophecy-ledgers all agreed: whoever charted the ninth iteration would lock reality into an inevitable cycle of collapse and rebirth. Henryk had blinded himself rather than risk completing it by accident. Tavin had taken up the work: drawing false geographies, teaching apprentices to map in circles, preserving contradiction as a form of resistance. Then the Counter-Archive's eldest scholar asked her to do something impossible: *document the eighth iteration*. Map what had existed before the Luminous Ascension rewrote the world. Not to enable the ninth—to understand the cycle itself. To find, in the gaps and silences of pre-Ascension memory, some escape clause, some proof that the iteration wasn't actually inevitable. Tavin spent three months in the hidden libraries, cross-referencing refugee testimony, bone-singer songs, and preserved starlight-glass that held impressions of the old stars. She found fragments. Whispers.
